questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what the frame around a painting can tell a researcher
questions.stem: In an architect's brief for a picture gallery, the question arises what the frame around a painting can tell the researcher.

options.text: The frame records the work's date, status and intended setting, since it was made for the picture.
The frame records the painter's working method, since the same carver served the workshop.
options.misconception: attributes the frame's evidence to the painter's hand

options.text: The frame records the subject of the picture, since the carving always illustrates the scene.
options.misconception: assumes carved frames always echo the subject

options.text: The frame records the size of the gallery, since frames were cut to fit the hanging spaces.
options.misconception: reads the frame as a measure of gallery dimensions

questions.explanation: A frame is made for a particular picture and carries its date, rank and expected place. The workshop, subject and gallery-size readings take the frame for evidence it does not register.
questions.hint: Ask what the frame was cut and fitted for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a work enters a national collection
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table pairing routes of accession with display decisions
questions.stem: A survey of a national collection's accessions for one year records the route of each and whether the object was publicly displayed; what does the table show?

options.text: That purchases and gifts brought in the same kind of object, since the museum accepted what it was given.
options.misconception: assumes gifts and purchases brought equivalent material

options.text: That objects entered by several routes, and the proportion put on display varied with the route taken.
That all accessioned objects went on display, since accessions are made for the public galleries.
options.misconception: claims full display where the table shows variation

options.text: That only bequests were displayed, since older material suits the taste of a public collection.
options.misconception: links display to age rather than to recorded routes

questions.explanation: The table records varied routes and a varied display rate, which is what distinguishes a working collection. The same-kind, all-displayed and bequests-only readings each flatten the columns.
questions.hint: Compare the route column with the display column.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an artist's self-presentation and later reception can diverge
questions.stem: An exhibition designer asks you to explain how an artist's self-presentation and later reception can diverge.

answer.exemplar: Self-presentation is the image the artist chose to put forward, often at the most flattering moment of a career, whereas later reception is assembled by critics, buyers and institutions over decades, so a reputation may rest on a small group of works or on a single early notice that later generations repeated, and the two histories can move in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: Self-presentation and later reception are made by different people at different times, so they can conflict. An account that treats the later reputation as the artist's intention misses two processes.
questions.hint: Ask who made each of the two accounts.

questions.learningObjective: Count the naming proposals recorded across a survey of catalogues
questions.stem: A survey of exhibition catalogues counts 4 naming proposals in the first decade, 3 in the second and 5 in the third; how many proposals does the survey record in total?
questions.explanation: Adding 4, 3 and 5 gives 12 proposals across the three decades. Treating the counts as changes between decades rather than totals for each would give a different figure.
questions.hint: Add the totals for the three decades together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a label history showing a term applied after the fact

stimulus.body: A gallery's label history shows that the pictures in one room were first described in 1904 as work of the old northern school, and that the phrase primitive northern first appears in a 1931 exhibition text, written by a curator who also noted that the term was borrowed from an earlier discussion of non-European art. A later label from 1968 uses the term without comment.

questions.stem: Given this label history, what does the survey establish?

options.text: That the 1931 curator invented the phrase, since no earlier discussion of any kind existed.
options.misconception: denies the borrowing the curator's note records

options.text: That the painters used the name among themselves, since the 1904 label already used similar wording.
options.misconception: reads similar wording as the same term in use

options.text: That the period name was applied later by a curator borrowing it, not used by the painters themselves.
That the 1968 label proves the name had become standard by then, since curators use only fixed terms.
options.misconception: treats one later usage as proof of general currency

questions.explanation: The label sequence shows a term entering later and being borrowed, with no evidence of contemporary use. The painters-used-it, invented-here and standard-by-1968 readings ignore the sequence.
questions.hint: Ask who first used the phrase and when.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what a manifesto asks of the people who follow it
questions.stem: Establish what a manifesto asks of its followers, then choose the option that describes it correctly.

options.text: It rejects the past entirely, so its value lies in denying what earlier artists had achieved.
options.misconception: makes denial the essential content of a manifesto

options.text: It lists the members of the group, so the programme is really a register of names.
options.misconception: reduces a manifesto to a list of members

options.text: It is a public request for money, so the programme is really an appeal for support.
options.misconception: treats a manifesto as a fundraising document

options.text: It sets a programme of shared aims and methods, so members can recognise the work it describes.

questions.explanation: A manifesto states aims and methods so that the work it claims can be recognised. The membership-list, appeal and pure-denial readings each misdescribe what it does.
questions.hint: Ask what a follower is expected to do after reading it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an attribution is argued rather than asserted
questions.stem: A curator asks how an attribution to a particular painter is argued rather than simply asserted.

options.text: By naming the most celebrated painter who could have done it, since fame settles the question.
options.misconception: treats reputation as a substitute for evidence

options.text: By weighing documents, style and material evidence, and stating the degree of certainty claimed.
By following the family tradition of owners, since long custody proves the maker's name.
options.misconception: mistakes custody for a record of authorship

options.text: By choosing the painter whose work the piece most resembles, since resemblance alone is the test.
options.misconception: treats resemblance as the whole of the argument

questions.explanation: An attribution is an argued case in which several kinds of evidence are weighed and the confidence stated. The fame, custody and resemblance-alone readings substitute a shortcut for an argument.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence is weighed and how certain the claim is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a comparison of lifetime and present descriptions of works
questions.stem: A survey of 24 works records how each was described at the maker's lifetime and how it is described now; what does the comparison show?

options.text: That the works are misattributed, since the two descriptions fail to agree with one another.
options.misconception: treats a change of description as evidence of misattribution

options.text: That the artist chose the later descriptions, since the wording simply improves over time.
options.misconception: attributes later wording to the artist who did not write it

options.text: That the framing of the maker has shifted, so later language often stresses qualities the artist did not claim.
That early descriptions are worthless, because only later viewers saw the works properly.
options.misconception: dismisses contemporary accounts as necessarily inferior

questions.explanation: The comparison shows reception developing its own vocabulary around the works. The author-chose, misattributed and worthless-early readings confuse change in description with change in authorship.
questions.hint: Ask who wrote each of the two descriptions.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a name for a group of painters comes to be fixed
questions.stem: A gallery curator explains how a name for a group of painters comes to be used and then fixed.

answer.exemplar: A label for a group of painters usually begins as a remark in a lecture or a review, is borrowed from an older debate, is repeated by critics who find it convenient, and is then fixed by a catalogue or a museum label, so the term that comes to seem descriptive was in fact a convenience adopted by a few writers and passed on.

questions.explanation: The naming process runs from a remark through repetition to institutional fixation. An account that treats a name as a natural description misses the accidents that produced it.
questions.hint: Trace the term from its first appearance to its later use.

questions.hint: Subtract the two named totals from the overall count.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret frame evidence when the present frame is not original

stimulus.body: A conservation note records that a portrait is set in a later frame of painted and gilded wood with a flat profile and a plain moulding, and that the original tacking holes around the panel correspond to a different, deeper frame that no longer survives. The note also records that the panel's back bears a dealer's label in ink.

questions.stem: Given this note, what does the frame evidence show?

options.text: That the dealer's label proves the frame was sold with the picture at the dealer's shop.
options.misconception: links a label on the panel to the provenance of the frame

options.text: That the present frame is original, because a flat profile is always the earliest moulding.
options.misconception: treats a profile shape as a fixed chronological marker

options.text: That the panel was never framed, since the surviving tacking holes point to a wall fixing.
options.misconception: reads fixings as evidence of a different display method

options.text: That the picture was once shown in a deeper frame and has since been reframed, so the present frame is later.

questions.explanation: Tacking holes for a deeper frame show an earlier setting, so the present frame is a replacement. The original, unframed and label-proves-frame readings each ignore the physical evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the current frame matches the fixings on the panel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a period name was used by the makers or applied later
questions.stem: Decide whether a period name was used by the makers or applied later, then choose the option that supports the decision.

options.text: If the term appears only in later records, the makers must have used it among themselves in private.
options.misconception: infers private usage from an absence in the record

options.text: If the term appears only in later records, the name is a retrospective label rather than a contemporary usage.
If the term appears only in later records, the works belong to a later period than the style suggests.
options.misconception: redates the works on the strength of a later label

options.text: If the term appears only in later records, no stylistic evidence can be used to date the works at all.
options.misconception: denies the value of style because a label is late

questions.explanation: A term found only in later sources is a retrospective label, not a contemporary usage. The private-usage, redating and no-evidence readings each overreach what a late attestation shows.
questions.hint: Ask when the term first appears in the record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what a written programme of aims amounts to in a group's history
questions.stem: An architect's client asks what a written programme of aims amounts to in the history of a group of artists.

options.text: A contract between the artists and a patron, so the programme is really a commercial arrangement.
options.misconception: treats a programme of aims as a commercial contract

options.text: A list of the members, so the group can be identified by reading the names on it.
options.misconception: reduces a programme of aims to a membership list

options.text: A statement of shared aims and methods that later readers use to recognise the work it claims.
A rulebook for the workshop, so its members could be required to paint in the prescribed manner.
options.misconception: makes a programme a binding rulebook

questions.explanation: A programme states aims and methods, and it becomes the test by which the work it claims is later judged. The membership-list, contract and rulebook readings each misidentify the document.
questions.hint: Ask what the document asks a reader to recognise.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey grading attributions by kind of evidence and confidence
questions.stem: A survey of 30 attributions records, for each, the kind of evidence used and whether the conclusion was stated as certain, likely or possible; what does it show?

options.text: That possible attributions are the most common, because researchers are generally cautious in print.
options.misconception: infers a printing habit from a distribution of claims

options.text: That all attributions are equally secure, since each dossier reaches some conclusion.
options.misconception: treats any conclusion as an equally strong one

options.text: That certain attributions rest on the strongest evidence, since certainty follows automatically from the record.
options.misconception: assumes certainty is a result rather than a choice

options.text: That attributions are graded in confidence, so a majority are argued rather than simply asserted.

questions.explanation: The dossier shows a range of confidence rather than a single standard, and a majority of argued cases. The equal-security, automatic-certainty and cautious-printing readings misdescribe the grading.
questions.hint: Read the confidence column before the evidence column.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a frame is treated as evidence rather than decoration
questions.stem: A gallery architect explains why the frame is treated as evidence rather than as decoration.

answer.exemplar: The frame is evidence because it was chosen and made for a particular picture, usually by a different hand from the painter, and often carved from a pattern of date; its moulding, its size, its gilding and its inscriptions therefore carry information about the picture's rank, its intended setting and the moment it was made, which the painted surface alone cannot supply.

questions.explanation: The frame records information about the picture's circumstances that the surface cannot. An account that calls it decoration misses the evidence a frame was made to carry.
questions.hint: Ask what the frame tells you that the paint does not.

questions.hint: Subtract the two recorded totals from the year's total.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare an artist's account of a work with later critical readings

stimulus.body: A review printed in 1912 describes an artist's late self-portrait as frank and unadorned, and the artist had described the same picture in a letter as a plain record of a face. A 1978 catalogue entry describes the same picture as having a studied simplicity, and notes that the picture was not seen in public between 1912 and 1978.

questions.stem: Given these records, what does the survey show about the two accounts?

options.text: That the artist's own letter proves the later catalogue is wrong, since the artist knew the picture best.
options.misconception: treats the artist's account as automatically correcting critics

options.text: That the later reading adds a claim the artist did not make, built on a picture unseen for most of a century.
That the two descriptions agree, since both of them call the picture plain and direct.
options.misconception: overreads a shared word as a shared judgement

options.text: That the picture was repainted between 1912 and 1978, since the description changed so much.
options.misconception: infers a repaint from a change in critical language

questions.explanation: The later description adds an interpretive claim after a long gap in public sight, which the artist's letter does not support. The artist-always-right, agreement and repaint readings each misread the records.
questions.hint: Note the gap in public sight between the two records.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Describe the role of the first person to use a label for a group
questions.stem: Establish who first used a label for a group of painters, then choose the option that describes that person's role.

options.text: A dealer who used it to market a group of works, so the term is primarily commercial.
options.misconception: reduces a label's first use to a sales device

options.text: A painter who named his own movement, so the term was made to be used from the beginning.
options.misconception: makes the first user the originator of the practice

options.text: A writer who offered it as a convenient description, later taken up by critics and then by institutions.
A government officer who defined a school of painting for official purposes in a later reform.
options.misconception: invents an official definition with no evidence

questions.explanation: The first user of a label typically offers a convenience that others adopt, and institutions then fix it. The painter, dealer and official readings each assign a role the record does not support.
questions.hint: Ask what the first user was trying to do with the word.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a later period name from a name used at the time
questions.stem: A museum educator asks how a period name applied afterwards differs from a name used at the time.

options.text: It is a legal category, since a period name fixes what may be sold as belonging to a period.
options.misconception: treats a stylistic label as a legal definition

options.text: It is more accurate, because scholars of later periods name things better than contemporaries did.
options.misconception: assumes later namers are automatically more accurate

options.text: It is a neutral description, since a name applied afterwards carries no argument of its own.
options.misconception: denies that a retrospective name makes a claim

options.text: It is a later label that organises works for description, rather than a term the makers themselves used.

questions.explanation: A retrospective name is a later tool for description, and it carries an argument about what belongs together. The more-accurate, neutral and legal-category readings each misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Ask who was doing the naming and when.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table comparing the scope, membership and claims of manifestos
questions.stem: A survey of manifestos records, for each, the number of stated aims, the number of members named and the number of works the programme claims; what does the table show?

options.text: That aims and membership are always equal in number, since a group lists one aim per member.
options.misconception: invents a numerical rule where the table shows none

options.text: That the programmes vary in scope, so a broad set of aims is not matched by a large membership.
That the most detailed programme claims the most works, since detail is a sign of influence.
options.misconception: links claim count to detail rather than to evidence

options.text: That manifestos were written to close groups, since naming members invites newcomers in.
options.misconception: reads an act of listing as an act of exclusion

questions.explanation: The table shows scope varying independently of membership, so a wide programme can come from a small group. The equal-numbers, detail-equals-influence and exclusion readings each override the columns.
questions.hint: Compare the aim column with the membership column.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a work enters a national collection
questions.learningObjective: Explain the sequence by which a work enters a national collection
questions.stem: A collections officer explains how a work actually enters a national collection.

answer.exemplar: Entry normally runs through a decision by the institution: an acquisition proposal setting out the work's importance and its condition, a recommendation by an advisory body, a decision by the governing body, and a legal transfer of ownership, and only after those steps is the object accessioned, catalogued and given its number, so the process is slow and selective rather than automatic.

questions.explanation: Entry is a sequence of proposals, recommendations, decisions and a legal transfer. An account that treats accessioning as a single automatic step loses the deliberation involved.
questions.hint: Ask what has to happen before a number is assigned.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the moulding width of a frame from two measured dimensions
questions.stem: A conservation survey measures an outer frame moulding 1.14 m wide and an inner sight edge 0.94 m across; how many centimetres of moulding lie on each side?
questions.explanation: The difference between outer and inner measures is 0.20 m, and dividing that by two sides gives 0.10 m, which is 10 cm of moulding on each side. Taking 0.20 m as one side would double the answer.
questions.hint: Halve the difference before converting to centimetres.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a programme sheet as a drafted and circulated document

stimulus.body: A programme sheet for a group of painters sets out a shared aim, lists the methods they would use, and names a set of works in which those methods appear. It also names three painters who are not among the signers, and a later editorial note states that the sheet was drafted by two people and circulated for comment before publication.

questions.stem: Given this programme sheet, what does the record show?

options.text: That the named painters are members, since a programme only names its own group.
options.misconception: assumes a programme names only its signatories

options.text: That it was a private letter, since it names painters who never read it.
options.misconception: treats a circulated programme as a private letter

options.text: That it is a drafted and circulated document, and that its claims reach beyond those who signed it.
That the sheet was written after the works it claims, since a claim can only follow the works.
options.misconception: reverses the relation between a claim and the work claimed

questions.explanation: The editorial note shows drafting and circulation, and the list of painters extends the claim past the signers. The private-letter, named-are-members and later-than-works readings each misread the document.
questions.hint: Weigh the editorial note against the list of names.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a statement belongs to self-presentation or to reception
questions.stem: Decide whether a statement of self-presentation belongs to the artist or to later viewers, then choose the option that matches.

options.text: If the artist described the work, every later description must repeat it, since influence is complete.
options.misconception: assumes later accounts must follow the artist's wording

options.text: If the artist described the work, the statement must be reception, since critics always quote the maker.
options.misconception: misplaces the artist's own words in the later account

options.text: If the artist chose the work, no statement about it can be called self-presentation at all.
options.misconception: denies the possibility of self-presentation on that basis

options.text: If the artist chose and described the work, the statement belongs to the self-presentation, not to reception.

questions.explanation: The artist's own choice and description belong to the self-presentation; later readings belong to reception. The misplaced-quote, no-self-presentation and complete-influence readings confuse the two.
questions.hint: Ask who made the choice being described.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a work enters a national collection
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an accession from a purchase
questions.stem: A national collection's registrar explains what distinguishes an accession from a purchase.

options.text: The accession is the act of buying, so a gift can never be accessioned by a national collection.
options.misconception: identifies accession with a single kind of transaction

options.text: The accession is the entry into the collection itself, which may follow a purchase, gift, bequest or transfer.
The accession is the moment a work is cleaned and restored for display in the galleries.
options.misconception: confuses accession with conservation work

options.text: The accession is the number printed on the work, so a record without a number proves no accession.
options.misconception: makes the identifier the substance of the event

questions.explanation: Accession is the entry of an object into the collection, whatever route it took. The purchase-only, conservation and number-only readings each reduce the term to something else.
questions.hint: Ask what has happened to the object at that moment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a comparison of first and current period labels
questions.stem: A survey of 20 works records the term used for each at its first publication and the term used in current catalogues; what does the comparison show?

options.text: That the current terms were chosen because the older ones had been forgotten by all readers.
options.misconception: invents collective forgetting as the cause of renaming

options.text: That the first terms are the accurate ones, since a cataloguer closer to the work knows it best.
options.misconception: assumes proximity guarantees accuracy in naming

options.text: That most works are now filed under period names that were not in use when they were first described.
That only the terminology has changed, since the works themselves remain untouched by the shift.
options.misconception: assumes naming has no effect on how works are grouped

questions.explanation: The comparison shows works now classified under later period names, which reorganises how they are discussed together. The accurate-first, forgotten-terms and terminology-only readings miss the regrouping.
questions.hint: Count works whose current label postdates the first description.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a programme of aims does for understanding a group
questions.stem: A gallery director explains what a programme of aims does for the understanding of a group of painters.

answer.exemplar: A programme of aims gives a group of painters a shared brief that can be used to explain their choices, because each decision can be read as a response to a stated aim, and it also provides the measure by which later viewers judge whether a particular work belongs to the group at all.

questions.explanation: A stated programme lets viewers explain and judge works by reference to shared aims. An account that treats it only as a rallying cry, or only as a curiosity, misses its working function.
questions.hint: Ask how a programme is used when a new work is judged.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total weight of evidence in an attribution dossier
questions.stem: A dossier weighs evidence: 4 documents of weight 2 points each, 5 stylistic observations of 1 point and 2 material analyses of 3 points; what is the total weight of points?
questions.explanation: The documents give 8 points, the observations 5 and the analyses 6, so the total is 19. Treating the material analyses as one combined test of 3 points would give 16 instead.
questions.hint: Multiply each count by its weight, then add the three totals.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Trace a name from a critic's card to institutional usage

stimulus.body: A critic's card found in an archive carries a date and the note: a name for the pictures in the room, a borrowing term from a discussion of craft in another country, and a remark that the name will not last. A gallery wall label from 1958 uses the same term, and a 1990 exhibition text refers to it as the name the critic introduced.

questions.stem: Given these records, what does the survey establish about the name?

options.text: That the term was a movement in its own right, since the 1990 text calls it a movement.
options.misconception: confuses a critical label with an organised group

options.text: That the critic had copied the term from the painters, since borrowing implies a prior source.
options.misconception: treats a borrowed word as a term used by the makers

options.text: That the name is unusable, since the critic predicted it would not last.
options.misconception: takes a contemporary opinion as the final verdict

options.text: That it was coined in criticism, with doubts at the time, and was later fixed by exhibition usage.

questions.explanation: The card, the wall label and the exhibition text together show a critical coinage, doubted at first and later fixed by usage. The copied, unusable and organised-movement readings misstate the sequence.
questions.hint: Read the three records in order of increasing date.

questions.learningObjective: State what a frame can be made to tell the researcher

options.text: The frame tells you the painter's mood on the day the picture was finished.
options.misconception: reads the frame as a record of the painter's state of mind

options.text: The frame's date, style and intended setting, since it was made for the picture it surrounds.
The frame shows the work was always considered finished, since frames are only made for complete works.
options.misconception: assumes frames are never made for unfinished work

options.text: The frame indicates the picture's exact value, since carved ornament was priced by the foot.
options.misconception: assumes a direct relation between ornament and price

questions.explanation: A frame records the circumstances the picture was valued in: when, in what style and for what place. The mood, always-finished and price readings each claim a precision the frame does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask what a frame was made to do for a picture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Define the self-presentation of an artist's work
questions.stem: A curator asks what is meant by the self-presentation of an artist's work.

options.text: The account written in the artist's workshop, whatever the artist actually intended by it.
options.misconception: makes the workshop rather than the artist the source of intention

options.text: The account that later critics gave, once the work had been seen by the public.
options.misconception: labels the critical account as the artist's own

options.text: The account the artist gave of their own aims and of the works offered as showing them.
The account a sitter gave of the portrait that was painted of them.
options.misconception: confuses the sitter's account with the artist's self-image

questions.explanation: Self-presentation is the account an artist gives of their aims and chosen works. The critics', workshop and sitter readings each locate it somewhere other than the artist.
questions.hint: Ask whose account of their own work it is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a comparison of stated aims with later critical credits
questions.stem: A survey of 25 works attributed to a group records for each the aims stated in the programme and the aims a later catalogue credits it with; what does it show?

options.text: That the programme was written after the works, since it matches the later readings so closely.
options.misconception: infers the programme's date from its fit with later readings

options.text: That the later catalogue is wrong in every case, since a maker's own programme is the only authority.
options.misconception: treats one document as the sole possible authority

options.text: That the works were changed after the programme was written, since a stated aim cannot change.
options.misconception: assumes a work cannot be re-read after it is made

options.text: That a number of works are read as expressing aims their makers did not state, often with added significance.

questions.explanation: Later readings often credit works with aims the programme never states, adding significance over time. The catalogue-wrong, changed-works and later-programme readings each misread the comparison.
questions.hint: Look for works credited with aims the programme omits.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the first use of a name for a movement matters
questions.stem: A museum's research guide explains why the first use of a name for a movement matters.

answer.exemplar: The first use of a name matters because it shows what the term was made to do, since a critic who borrows a word from another debate is solving a problem of description at that moment, and the later history of the term, its adoption by institutions and its eventual use as a period label, all grow out of that initial convenience.

questions.explanation: The first use reveals the term's purpose and the problem it was solving. An account that begins with the settled modern label loses the accidents that shaped it.
questions.hint: Ask what problem the first user was trying to solve.

questions.hint: Subtract the short restatements from the total number of points.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a record of changing display groupings under a period name

stimulus.body: A gallery's exhibition history shows that pictures grouped under a period name in 1935 were displayed with pictures of a different origin in 1958 and again with a wider range in 1971, and that the labels changed each time. A 1958 curator's note explains that the new grouping was chosen because a visiting delegation wanted to see a single national tradition.

questions.stem: Given this exhibition history, what does the survey show?

options.text: That the 1958 grouping was a correction of earlier error, since the curators had discovered the right picture.
options.misconception: reads a practical regrouping as a scholarly correction

options.text: That the period name was a working arrangement for display, changed to meet a stated need.
That the 1971 range proves the earlier group was dishonest, since curators concealed the real history.
options.misconception: infers deliberate concealment from a change of range

options.text: That the period name describes a fixed group, since no display arrangement should change over time.
options.misconception: treats a display label as a permanent category

questions.explanation: The grouping was a display decision taken for a stated reason and later altered again. The correction, dishonesty and fixed-group readings impose a permanent meaning on a working label.
questions.hint: Read the curator's note before drawing conclusions.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which stage of the accession process a document records
questions.stem: Establish which stage of the accession process a document records, then choose the option that identifies it.

options.text: A recommendation by an advisory body records a sale, since a recommendation follows the purchase.
options.misconception: puts a recommendation after the transaction it precedes

options.text: A recommendation by an advisory body is a decision, since the body holds the final authority.
options.misconception: gives an advisory body the final deciding power

options.text: A recommendation by an advisory body records a proposal, not a decision, since the decision follows separately.
A recommendation by an advisory body means the work is already catalogued, since the number follows at once.
options.misconception: assumes cataloguing follows a recommendation immediately

questions.explanation: A recommendation is one step in a sequence that ends in a decision and then a transfer. The decision, sale and already-catalogued readings each collapse the stages.
questions.hint: Ask whether the text decides anything or only advises.

options.text: A set of rules for the workshop, so apprentices copied the manner their masters had set out.
options.misconception: makes a programme a rulebook for apprentices

options.text: A list of prices, so each member knew what his panel would earn from the exhibition.
options.misconception: reads a programme of aims as a schedule of fees

options.text: A set of measurements, so the panels would match when hung together on one wall.
options.misconception: confuses a programme with a technical specification

options.text: A shared programme of aims, so the group's members could work to a common brief and be recognised by it.

questions.explanation: A programme gave members a common aim and a means of being recognised as a group. The prices, measurements and rulebook readings mistake a statement of purpose for something administrative.
questions.hint: Ask what the members of a group share after reading it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table of frame materials, methods and originality
questions.stem: A survey of 30 frames records for each the material, whether it is carved or moulded, and whether it is original to the picture; what does the table show?

options.text: That carved frames are always later, since moulding was a later invention than carving.
options.misconception: asserts a false order of invention between techniques

options.text: That a number of pictures have been reframed, since the frames recorded differ from the original fittings.
That all thirty frames are original, since the survey only records frames still in place.
options.misconception: ignores the reframed cases the table records

options.text: That frame material follows the subject, since painted panels received carved frames and prints moulded ones.
options.misconception: invents a subject-based rule for frame materials

questions.explanation: Where the recorded frame differs from the original fittings, the picture has been reframed. The technique-order, all-original and subject-rule readings each override what the table shows.
questions.hint: Look for the rows where the frame is not original.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a name for a movement becomes fixed yet remains contingent
questions.stem: A label writer asks you to explain how a name for a movement can become fixed while remaining contingent.

answer.exemplar: A name becomes fixed when writers, dealers and institutions repeat it until it seems the only word for the works, and it remains contingent because the first use was a choice made for local reasons, so the settled label still carries the assumptions of a particular critic, a particular decade and a particular argument about what the works had in common.

questions.explanation: Institutional repetition makes a label look inevitable, while its origin in particular circumstances keeps it arguable. An account that treats a fixed name as self-evident loses the arguments inside it.
questions.hint: Ask how a convenient label becomes the only word available.

questions.hint: Add the two documented groups, leaving the stylistic one out.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a dossier that assembles a case while stating its limits

stimulus.body: A dossier summary lists a panel's ownership in 1730, 1810 and 1920; records that the panel was lined in a nineteenth-century campaign; notes that the 1920 owner was a dealer of some standing; and observes that the panel's paint is consistent with works produced for that dealer around 1890. The summary states no document naming the painter, and no other name is attached to the panel.

questions.stem: Given this dossier, what does it establish?

options.text: That the nineteenth-century lining proves the panel was painted in the nineteenth century.
options.misconception: takes a later campaign as the date of painting

options.text: That the panel is certainly by the dealer, since a dealer owns and therefore makes the work.
options.misconception: conflates ownership with authorship

options.text: That a case for one attribution can be built from period, ownership and material evidence, though it is not certain.
That the panel cannot be discussed at all, since no document names the painter.
options.misconception: denies that evidence can be weighed without a naming document

questions.explanation: The dossier assembles a case from date, ownership, treatment and material fit, while stating its limits. The dealer-painted, lining-date and nothing-to-say readings overreach or dismiss the evidence.
questions.hint: Note both the evidence assembled and the limits stated.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Separate self-presentation from later reception in an account
questions.stem: Decide which parts of an account are self-presentation and which are later reception, then choose the option that matches.

options.text: Both are self-presentation, since a work only means what its maker intended it to mean.
options.misconception: reduces all meaning to intention

options.text: The artist's chosen subjects are reception, because reception covers everything said about a work.
options.misconception: widens reception to cover the artist's own choices

options.text: Later critical framing is self-presentation, since by then the artist had become part of the tradition.
options.misconception: moves later criticism into the artist's own account

options.text: The artist's chosen subjects and his own statements are self-presentation; the critical framing added since is reception.

questions.explanation: Self-presentation covers the artist's own choices and statements; reception covers what was added afterwards. The widened, reversed and intention-only readings blur the boundary the two accounts mark.
questions.hint: Ask who is speaking in each part of the account.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why period frames are shown as part of a display
questions.stem: An architect's client asks why the frames in a period room are often shown as part of the display.

options.text: Because a frame protects the picture, and the display simply shows how that protection is achieved.
options.misconception: reduces the frame to a protective function only

options.text: Because a frame carries evidence of the picture's date, rank and setting that the surface alone cannot give.
Because frames in a period room are usually better made than the pictures they surround.
options.misconception: assumes a general superiority of frames over pictures

options.text: Because frames were cheaper than pictures, so a room of frames is a sign of a modest patron.
options.misconception: infers a patron's means from the presence of frames

questions.explanation: A frame is shown because it is evidence of the picture's circumstances, not merely a border or a lid. The protection, better-made and cheaper readings reduce the frame to a secondary function.
questions.hint: Ask what the frame records that the picture cannot.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a work enters a national collection
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a comparison of dates of making and dates of entry
questions.stem: A collection's survey records for 30 accessions the route, the year of entry and the year the object was made; what does the comparison show?

options.text: That every accession is recent, since the survey covers only the last year of acquisitions.
options.misconception: assumes a narrow date range without support

options.text: That the collection was assembled to preserve recent work, since most objects enter as soon as they are made.
options.misconception: reads a gap as evidence of preference for new work

options.text: That objects entered long after they were made, so the collection's history is separate from the objects' histories.
That the route of acquisition depends on how old the object is, since older objects always arrive as gifts.
options.misconception: asserts a route and age link the survey does not show

questions.explanation: The gap between making and entry shows the collection accumulating objects with lives of their own. The recent-work, all-recent and route-depends-on-age readings override the two year columns.
questions.hint: Compare the year made with the year of entry.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a later period name remains useful when it is imperfect
questions.stem: A catalogue editor explains why a period name applied afterwards can be useful even when it is inaccurate.

answer.exemplar: A retrospective period name is useful because it gives a workable way to group and discuss works that were made without any such group in mind, and even an imperfect name is a shared reference that allows argument to begin; what matters is that the editor says when the label was applied and what it was applied to.

questions.explanation: A later label offers a shared handle even when it is imprecise, provided its date and scope are stated. An account that dismisses such labels forgoes the shared reference they create.
questions.hint: Ask what the label makes possible for readers.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a surviving fragment of a programme sheet

stimulus.body: A surviving fragment of a programme sheet states an aim in the first person, names two methods, and refers to a third artist without any comment, and the sheet is written in a hand identified elsewhere as that of a scribe working for two different painters. A catalogue note records that the fragment was used as a wrapping sheet in a bookseller's stock.

questions.stem: Given this fragment, what does the record show?

options.text: That the aims were abandoned immediately, since the sheet was later used for wrapping.
options.misconception: infers rejection of the aims from later reuse

options.text: That the fragment proves the two painters agreed on every aim, since one hand wrote the whole sheet.
options.misconception: treats one scribe as evidence of full agreement

options.text: That the sheet was a private letter between two friends, since it speaks in the first person.
options.misconception: reads a first-person programme as private correspondence

options.text: That a statement of aims existed, was made in a shared working context, and was later reused as an ordinary object.

questions.explanation: The fragment records a statement of aims made within a shared working arrangement, later reused and thus degraded as a document. The agreement, private-letter and abandoned-aims readings overreach.
questions.hint: Read the hand and the reuse note together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what an attribution argues from and how it concludes
questions.stem: Establish what an attribution argues from, then choose the option that describes a properly stated conclusion.

options.text: It argues from documents, style and materials, and it must therefore state a definite name without doubt.
options.misconception: conflates weighing evidence with claiming certainty

options.text: It argues from documents, style and materials, and it states how far the evidence carries the claim.
It argues from style alone, since documents and materials always mislead the enquiry.
options.misconception: discards two kinds of evidence without reason

options.text: It argues from the collector's taste, since a good collection is the surest guide to authorship.
options.misconception: substitutes collection taste for evidence

questions.explanation: A stated attribution weighs several kinds of evidence and is explicit about the degree of confidence it claims. The certainty, style-only and taste-based readings each misstate what a sound attribution requires.
questions.hint: Ask both what it argues from and how firmly it concludes.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes an attribution a hypothesis rather than a fact
questions.stem: A museum's research officer asks what makes an attribution a hypothesis rather than a fact.

options.text: That it names a painter of moderate reputation, since famous names attract less scrutiny.
options.misconception: judges an attribution by the fame of the name

options.text: That it is written down, since an unwritten judgement can never be provisional.
options.misconception: makes the written form the sign of provisionality

options.text: That it rests on a weighing of evidence that could be altered by new documents, materials or finds.
That it disagrees with the museum's catalogue, since a hypothesis must differ from the record.
options.misconception: defines provisionality as disagreement with the record

questions.explanation: An attribution is a hypothesis because the evidence behind it can change, not because of how it is written or who it names. The written, reputation and disagreement readings misidentify what makes a claim provisional.
questions.hint: Ask what new evidence could do to the claim.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table of joinery, timber and maker's marks in frames
questions.stem: A survey of 24 frames records the joinery method, the timber and the maker's mark; what does the table show?

options.misconception: links a frame shop to the painting workshop

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a work enters a national collection
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes entry into a national collection a deliberate process
questions.stem: A registrar explains to a student what makes entry into a national collection a deliberate process.

answer.exemplar: Entry is deliberate because the institution must judge significance, condition and legal title before accepting an object, and each of those judgements can refuse it, so the collection's shape reflects a series of decisions about what is worth holding in the public interest, which is why acquisitions of the same period and quality can differ so widely between institutions.

questions.explanation: Significance, condition and title can each block an acquisition, so a collection records decisions. An account that treats entry as automatic misses the judgement involved.
questions.hint: Ask what could have stopped the acquisition at any stage.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Trace a term from a provisional critical use to a fixed label

stimulus.body: A press clipping of 1912 uses a new term for a group of pictures, explains that the term has no settled meaning and says it is used only for convenience. A 1935 catalogue lists the pictures under that term in a room title. A 1974 review uses the term with an implied definition and no explanation of where it came from.

questions.stem: From the clipping, the catalogue and the review, what does the survey show?

options.text: That the pictures always belonged to a settled group, since the 1935 catalogue places them together.
options.misconception: takes a later arrangement as proof of an earlier certainty

options.text: That a provisional convenience became a fixed label, and that the later use quietly assumes what the first use denied.
That the 1974 reviewer changed the meaning deliberately, since the term had become a label by then.
options.misconception: supposes an intention the clipping does not record

options.text: That the term should not be used, since it was introduced as a convenience rather than a description.
options.misconception: treats the admission of convenience as a reason for ban

questions.explanation: A term offered as provisional became a fixed room title and then an assumed definition, and the later use carries the certainty the first refused. The always-group, deliberate-change and unusable readings miss the drift.
questions.hint: Compare the caution in 1912 with the certainty in 1974.

questions.learningObjective: Describe how a later period name should properly be used

options.misconception: treats a later label as a surviving usage

options.text: It is a retrospective label that groups works, so the date of coinage is of no interest to a reader.
options.misconception: dismisses the date of coinage as irrelevant

options.text: It is a retrospective label that groups works for discussion, and its date of coinage should be stated.
It is a neutral description, so it needs no date, no scope and no note of its making.
options.misconception: denies that a label makes a claim of its own

questions.explanation: A retrospective label works as a shared reference, and stating when it was coined keeps its claims open to examination. The irrelevant-date, surviving-usage and neutral-description readings remove what makes it useful.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs to know to use the label well.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compare an artist's own description of a work with later critical accounts

stimulus.body: A letter from an artist to a dealer describes a picture as a plain record of a face, done in a single week, and the same artist is later described in a 1930 monograph as having made the work as an essay in the new simplicity. A 1950 review treats the picture as a manifesto of restraint. The letter is dated two years before the picture was first exhibited.

questions.stem: From the letter and the later writings, what does the survey show about the picture's reception?

options.text: That the 1930 and 1950 accounts are both wrong, since neither was written by the artist himself.
options.misconception: discards later readings merely because of their authorship

options.text: That the letter settles the interpretation, since a maker's own words override all later critics.
options.misconception: makes the artist's words the final authority on the work

options.text: That the artist's own account and later accounts differ in kind, so a later reading may add a claim he did not make.
That the picture was painted two years after the letter, since the letter describes the finished work.
options.misconception: reverses the order of a description and a painting

questions.explanation: The letter gives a plain account of method, while the monograph and review build an argument on the work. The settles-it, both-wrong and reversed-date readings each misread the record.
questions.hint: Compare what the artist claimed with what later writers claimed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State what a frame's evidence can and cannot establish
questions.stem: Establish what a frame's evidence can and cannot show, then choose the option that says so correctly.

options.text: A frame settles attribution, because a frame is made by the same workshop that painted the picture.
options.misconception: assumes the frame shop and the picture shop are one

options.text: A frame supports claims about date, rank and setting, and it also usually names the painter in its label.
options.misconception: assumes a frame carries a maker's name in every case

options.text: A frame establishes nothing, since a frame can be replaced at any time without trace being left.
options.misconception: dismisses the evidence a frame can carry

options.text: A frame supports claims about date, rank and setting, and it cannot by itself establish who painted the picture.

questions.explanation: A frame documents circumstance, not authorship, and it may be replaced while leaving useful traces. The naming, nothing-shows and settles-attribution readings overstate or dismiss its evidence.
questions.hint: Ask what a frame is made of, and what it is cut for.
